summary: In the Nazareth synagogue, Jesus reads Isaiah’s promise and declares it fulfilled; when He speaks of God’s mercy to Gentiles, His hometown tries to throw Him off a cliff.
key_insight: Jesus stopped reading in the middle of Isaiah’s sentence. The next words were “the day of vengeance of our God.” He proclaimed “the acceptable year of the LORD” and left the day of judgment unread.
story: Jesus came to Nazareth, where He had been brought up. As His custom was, He went into the synagogue on the Sabbath day and stood up to read. He was handed the book of the prophet Isaiah, and He found the place where it was written:

“The Spirit of the LORD is upon Me, Because He has anointed Me To preach the gospel to the poor.” The passage went on: He was sent to heal the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives and recovery of sight to the blind, to set the oppressed free, and “To proclaim the acceptable year of the LORD.”
Then He closed the book, gave it back to the attendant and sat down. Every eye in the synagogue was fixed on Him. He began, “Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing.”

All of them spoke well of Him and marveled at the gracious words that came from His mouth. Yet they said, “Is this not Joseph’s son?” Jesus answered what they were thinking: “You will surely say this proverb to Me, ‘Physician, heal yourself! Whatever we have heard done in Capernaum, do also here in Your country.’ ” Then He said, “Assuredly, I say to you, no prophet is accepted in his own country.”

He reminded them of their own Scriptures. There were many widows in Israel in Elijah’s day, when the heavens were shut and famine covered the land, yet Elijah was sent to none of them except a widow in Zarephath, in the region of Sidon. There were many lepers in Israel in Elisha’s time, yet none was cleansed except Naaman the Syrian.

At this, everyone in the synagogue was filled with wrath. They rose up, drove Him out of the town and led Him to the brow of the hill on which Nazareth was built, intending to throw Him down over the cliff. “Then passing through the midst of them, He went His way.”

fit.question: Matthew 13:54–58 and Mark 6:1–6 also tell of Jesus rejected in His hometown, later in His ministry. Is Luke telling that same visit early, or did Nazareth reject Him twice?

points.label: Two visits
points.text: The outcomes differ. Here the town tries to kill Jesus at the start of His Galilean work; in Matthew and Mark there is no attempt on His life, and Mark says His disciples were with Him and that He healed a few sick people and marveled at their unbelief. The Capernaum works mentioned here (Luke 4:23) could include the nobleman’s son, healed in Capernaum before this (John 4:46–54). This harmony follows the two-visit reading (see event 64).

points.label: One visit, placed first
points.text: McGarvey and others think Luke tells the same visit at the front of his account because it sums up Jesus’ mission and its rejection. They note that Luke 4:23 mentions works in Capernaum that Luke has not yet described, and that both accounts share the question about His family and the saying about a prophet in his own country.

fit.note: Whether Nazareth heard Him once or twice, the accounts agree on what happened and why, and neither reading requires an error.
fit.short: Many see two visits, Luke’s early and Matthew and Mark’s later; others think Luke placed one visit first. Views differ.

fit.question: Jesus says the heavens were shut “three years and six months” in Elijah’s day. But 1 Kings 18:1 says the word of the LORD came to Elijah “in the third year.” Which is it?

points.label: Different starting points
points.text: The drought began with Elijah’s word to Ahab (1 Kings 17:1). Elijah then hid by the brook Cherith until it dried up (17:7) before going to Zarephath. “The third year” in 18:1 most likely counts from a point inside the drought, such as his stay in Zarephath, not from its beginning.

points.label: A second witness
points.text: James also says it did not rain “for three years and six months” (James 5:17). Kings dates one moment; Jesus and James give the length of the whole drought.

fit.note: Kings and Luke measure different things. Nothing here requires an error.
fit.short: Kings dates a moment “in the third year,” probably of Elijah’s stay in Zarephath; the whole drought lasted longer, as James 5:17 agrees.

scene.label: The synagogue service
scene.text: A Sabbath service included prayers, a reading from the Law, a reading from the Prophets, and often a word of teaching. A visitor could be invited to speak (Acts 13:15). The reader stood out of respect for Scripture, then sat down to teach, as Jesus did.

scene.label: The scroll
scene.text: Books were scrolls. Jesus unrolled Isaiah near its end and found the place He wanted. Luke’s wording follows the Greek Old Testament and draws in a line from Isaiah 58:6 about setting the oppressed free.

scene.label: The acceptable year
scene.text: Isaiah’s words echo the Year of Jubilee, when every fiftieth year Israel was to “proclaim liberty throughout all the land” (Leviticus 25:10). Slaves went free and family land returned to its owners.

scene.label: Elijah and Elisha
scene.text: The widow of Zarephath (1 Kings 17:8–16) and Naaman the Syrian (2 Kings 5:1–14) were both Gentiles. In both stories, God’s prophet blessed an outsider while many in Israel went without.

scene.label: Nazareth’s hill
scene.text: Nazareth was a small village built on a hillside in lower Galilee, with limestone slopes and drops around it. Later tradition points to a cliff outside the town, but Luke says only that it was the brow of the hill on which the town stood.

witnesses.luke: Luke alone tells this scene in full and places it at the very start of Jesus’ public ministry. It gathers the themes of his whole Gospel: the Spirit’s anointing, good news for the poor, release for captives, grace reaching Gentiles, and rejection by Jesus’ own people. The same pattern returns in Acts, where the message rejected in synagogues goes out to the Gentiles (Acts 13:46).

seeing.reveals: Jesus claims to be the Spirit-anointed One of Isaiah 61, the Messiah who brings good news to the poor and liberty to captives. His grace is wide enough to reach a Sidonian widow and a Syrian general.
seeing.living: Nazareth admired His gracious words until grace reached past them to outsiders. Receive Jesus as the One who sets you free, and rejoice that His mercy is not limited to people like you. The good news for the poor is good news for anyone who knows he is poor.
seeing.ponder: Is there anyone you would be offended to see Jesus bless before you?

preaching.big_idea: The gracious words that amazed Nazareth enraged it when grace reached the outsider.
preaching.watch_for: Watch the crowd turn. In verse 22 “all bore witness to Him”; in verse 28 “all those in the synagogue” are filled with wrath. The turn comes when Jesus points to God’s mercy on Gentiles in Israel’s own Scriptures.
